answer_summary: Ho frames optogenetics as timely because retinal gene therapy has been validated by Luxturna and by broader gene-therapy approvals. He compares current optogenetics to the evolution from early wet AMD treatments to modern anti-VEGF therapy: newer optogenetic proteins are faster, broader across visible light, and may give patients with advanced retinal or macular degeneration more realistic hope.

answer_summary: Ho says retinal gene therapy is moving from rare inherited disease into common retina diseases such as wet AMD, with evidence that anti-VEGF-like proteins can be produced durably rather than delivered as repeated injection peaks. He does not expect injections to disappear; he sees gene therapy as a possible foundation therapy for selected high-burden patients, with injections still used as needed, and notes cost/access questions remain secondary to proving better long-term vision.

answer_summary: Ho used exam findings, visual acuity, OCT, and sometimes fluorescein angiography to decide when ranibizumab retreatment was needed. He thought it was unlikely that a new monotherapy would replace ranibizumab within 5 years, but combinations including ranibizumab might improve outcomes, and he supported a Lucentis-versus-Avastin head-to-head study while criticizing its slow launch.
